what_its_for: This medicine is a combination birth control pill (oral contraceptive) used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two hormones — a progestin (norgestimate) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) — that work together to stop ovulation (the release of an egg), thicken cervical mucus to block sperm, and thin the uterine lining. Some brands are also approved to treat moderate acne in females who are at least 15 years old and have already started their periods.
how_to_take: Take one pill by mouth every day at the same time each day. Pick a time that is easy for you to remember, such as with breakfast or at bedtime. Swallow the pill whole with or without food. If the pill upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal or at bedtime. Follow the pills in the pack in order — never skip pills or take them out of order. Most packs contain 28 pills: 21 active (hormone) pills and 7 inactive (reminder) pills. Start a new pack right away after finishing the current one, even if your period has not ended yet.
dosing: Take one pill every day for 28 days, then start a new pack immediately. Take the pills in the exact order shown on the pack. Active hormone pills are taken for 21 days, followed by 7 reminder (placebo) pills. Your period will usually come during the reminder pill week. Always start a new pack on the same day of the week as you started the first pack. If this is your first pack ever, you may need to use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days.
missed_dose: Missing pills increases your risk of pregnancy. If you miss 1 active pill, take it as soon as you remember, even if that means taking 2 pills in one day. Then continue taking the rest of the pack as normal. No backup birth control is needed. If you miss 2 active pills in a row in Week 1 or Week 2, take 2 pills on the day you remember and 2 pills the next day, then continue 1 pill per day. Use a backup method (like condoms) for the next 7 days. If you miss 2 active pills in a row in Week 3, or if you miss 3 or more active pills at any time, throw away the rest of the pack and start a new pack that same day. Use backup birth control for the next 7 days. If you had unprotected sex during missed pills, contact your doctor right away. You may need emergency contraception. Reminder (placebo) pills do not contain hormones — it is okay to skip them, but try to stay on schedule.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use pills that are expired — check the expiration date on the package. Dispose of unused or expired pills properly — do not flush them down the toilet unless the label says it is safe to do so.
what_to_avoid: Do not smoke while taking this medicine, especially if you are over 35 years old. Smoking greatly increases your risk of serious blood clots, heart attack, and stroke. Avoid taking this medicine if you are pregnant or think you might be pregnant. Some medicines can make birth control pills less effective, including certain antibiotics (like rifampin), seizure medicines, HIV medicines, and herbal supplements like St. John's Wort — always tell all your doctors and pharmacists that you are on birth control pills. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it may affect how the medicine works. Limit alcohol, as it may increase your risk of side effects. Do not skip pills or take them out of order.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have any of these warning signs — remember the acronym ACHES: Abdominal pain (severe stomach pain), Chest pain or shortness of breath, Headaches that are severe or sudden, Eye problems (blurred vision, loss of vision, or flashing lights), Severe leg pain or swelling (especially in the calf). Also contact your doctor if you have: yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), a lump in your breast, heavy or unusual vaginal bleeding, signs of a severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of face or throat, difficulty breathing), your period is more than 2 weeks late and you have missed any pills, or if you have any new or worsening symptoms that concern you. Tell your doctor before starting this medicine if you have a history of blood clots, stroke, heart attack, high blood pressure, migraine with aura, liver disease, or breast cancer.
when_it_works: If you start this medicine on the first day of your period, it works right away. If you start on any other day, it takes about 7 days to become fully effective — use a backup birth control method (like condoms) during those first 7 days. For acne treatment, it may take 3 to 6 months before you see improvement. Keep taking the pill every day as directed, even if you do not notice changes right away.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking it, stop taking it and call your doctor immediately. Breastfeeding: This medicine is generally not recommended right after giving birth or while breastfeeding, as it may reduce your milk supply. Talk to your doctor about the best birth control option if you are breastfeeding. Teens: This medicine can be used in teenagers who have already started their periods and need birth control or acne treatment. Adults over 35 who smoke: This medicine is NOT recommended — the risk of serious heart and blood vessel problems is too high. Older adults: This medicine is not typically used after menopause. Liver problems: Do not use if you have active liver disease or liver tumors. Kidney or heart disease: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine.
